title: Zeal in amending (I.25)
hookLine: keep watch over yourself with steady zeal
tomorrow: is the kingdom of God a place you can point to?

lines: HOT IN JANUARY, COLD BY FEBRUARY.
IF ONLY I KNEW I'D PERSEVERE.
cards: January resolutions burn hot. Some of them are cold by February. Big promises often go that way: a burst, a slip, then quiet.
The Imitation tells a story about a man who wanted a guarantee before he'd fully commit. He knelt before an altar, worn out with worry, and said: if only I knew that I would persevere!
Then, the book says, he heard an answer inside him. It wasn't a guarantee. It was a question.

teach.h: DO NOW WHAT YOU'D DO THEN.
teach.b: What would you do if you knew? Do now what you'd do then, and you'll be secure. That's the answer the man heard, and the book says his anxious wavering stopped.
He quit prying into the future and looked for what God wanted, to begin and finish each good work.
That's the Imitation's zeal: not a bonfire, a watch. Keep watch over yourself, chapter twenty-five says, stir yourself up, warn yourself, and whatever happens to others, don't neglect yourself.
What bothers you in someone else, avoid in yourself. Steady, not loud. The book even admits the cost: you'll make progress, it says, in proportion to the effort you put into yourself.
A neighbor tradition says something close.

teach.h: AN ISLAND NO FLOOD CAN OVERWHELM.
teach.b: In the Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings, Max Müller's translation reads: "By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm."
Both picture change as watchfulness kept up day after day, not one heroic vow. Both put the work close to home: yourself first, not your neighbor.

The man in the Imitation finds his peace by handing the future to God's will and asking grace to begin. The Dhammapada's verse names no God to lean on; the rousing and the island are the wise person's own.
Two old answers to the same January question, each in its own words.

how: Catholics make a 'firm purpose of amendment' in confession, resolving with God's help to change, and many renew such resolutions in a daily examination of conscience.

o: strict rules enforced on everyone around you
a burst of passion that changes everything
steady watchfulness in setting your life right

games.q: the man at the altar, and a neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: if only I knew I would persevere
do now what you'd do then
an island no flood can overwhelm

s: zeal in the Imitation means loud, fiery enthusiasm
it's steady watchfulness: watch over yourself, stir yourself up, warn yourself.
the Dhammapada pictures the earnest person making an island
an island which no flood can overwhelm, in Max Müller's translation.
the Imitation and the Dhammapada say exactly the same thing
both prize daily watchfulness; the Imitation leans on God's will and grace, the verse on the wise person's own effort.

games.q: you've started three workout plans this year and dropped every one. what does the answer the man at the altar heard suggest?
o: skip the guarantee; do today's step as if you knew you'd keep going.
wait until you're sure you'll stick with it before starting again.
make a stricter plan so that quitting feels impossible.
games.why: he wanted certainty first. the answer was: do now what you'd do if you knew, and you'll be secure.

practice: Choose one small habit you'd like to amend. Name what you want, then the obstacle that usually trips you, then one plan: when that moment comes, I'll do this instead. Keep it small enough to start today.
Hold the plan quietly for the sit, and if you pray, place it in God's hands.

wordCard.voice: Zeal in amending. The Imitation's counsel: keep watch over yourself, and set your life right steadily, one good work at a time, starting now.

orig.note: Latin: amendment, setting right; the word in the chapter's Latin title, de ferventi emendatione totius vitae nostrae.

carryVoice: Your line: steady zeal. A watch kept every day outlasts a vow shouted once. That's today.

sources.q: By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.
